strengths: Identifies and quantifies a genuine, previously under-explored failure mode of GUI agents: unreliable execution of toggle/state-control instructions, with systematic evidence of a toggling bias (high N-FPTR, near-100% P-TMR but low P-AMR) across both proprietary (GPT-5, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and open-source agents.

Constructs a large-scale state-control benchmark (81,836 samples; 8,184 test) from multiple public datasets with a three-step annotation pipeline, inter-annotator agreement between two independent MLLMs, a theoretical analysis of agreement-based label reliability (Table 4), and manual verification of 200 samples.

Evaluation is thorough and well-controlled: comparisons against zero-shot baselines, state-focused prompting, StaR-style prompting, and ground-truth-state upper bounds (Table 9), component ablations (Table 10), four target agents with different architectures/history strategies, three general agentic benchmarks, and a dynamic AndroidWorld-based evaluation.

The main results are convincing: large O-AMR gains (up to ~36 points), N-AMR rising to ~96-97% for all agents, and evidence that training (not prompting) is necessary, which directly addresses the annotator-paradox argument in the introduction.

The paper shows the method does not trade off general agentic performance (preserved or improved on AndroidControl, AITZ, GUI-Odyssey), with honest reporting of degradations (AgentCPM-GUI-8B on AITZ/GUI-Odyssey) and an error analysis attributing them to model-specific coordinate drift rather than StaR.
Reproducibility appears strong: prompt templates, hyperparameters, metric definitions, and data splits are all provided, with code and benchmark released.
weaknesses: Benchmark label noise and potential correlated annotator errors: test labels come from two MLLMs whose errors may be correlated (both are general VLMs); only 200 instances are manually verified, and the reported ~91% state-label accuracy implies a nontrivial error floor that could distort the key O-AMR metric, especially since N-AMR is measured against these labels.

Severe data-source imbalance: AITW contributes ~93% of training samples (68,380/73,652) and test samples (7,558/8,184), so the benchmark's diversity claims are only partially supported and results may be dominated by one dataset's UI style.

The core method is a structured chain-of-thought SFT template (perceive/analyze/decide); this is a natural and somewhat incremental extension of existing CoAT-style reasoning for GUI agents (e.g., AITZ, chain-of-action agents). The primary novelty lies in the problem identification and benchmark rather than the method.

Potential circularity: Qwen-2-VL-72B serves both as a benchmark annotator and as an evaluated agent, and StaR training data are constructed to mirror the benchmark's exact decision rule and reasoning template, raising the concern that a large part of the gains reflects fitting the benchmark's label-generation process rather than broadly improved toggle reasoning. Generalization to unseen toggle styles/UI families is not tested.

The dynamic evaluation is very small (20 tasks), all authored by the paper itself and toggle-centric, limiting the strength of the real-world applicability claim; no variance or repeated-run statistics are reported for it or for the main results.

Some metric choices deviate from community standards without sensitivity analysis: the 4% coordinate threshold for toggle clicks (vs. the standard 14%) is justified by fine-grained widgets but is not ablated, and N-FPR semantics (requiring exact coordinate coincidence) are unusual.

Minor presentation issues: repeated wording of claims, some typos ('Trun on alarm', 'finshed()'), and Table 3/benchmark naming inconsistencies (GUI-Odyssey cited as [34] in the appendix but [23] elsewhere).

strengths: Identifies a concrete, well-motivated and previously under-explored failure mode of GUI agents: unreliable toggle state reasoning, with a clean taxonomy of false-positive vs. false-negative toggling and a comprehensive 8-metric evaluation suite (O/P/N-TMR/AMR/FNR/FPR).

The state control benchmark is large (81,836 samples from six public datasets) and the annotation pipeline is documented in detail, including a thoughtful theoretical analysis of inter-annotator agreement (Eqs. 5-6, Table 4) justifying that agreement filtering improves label quality over a single MLLM annotator.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this kind of work: zero-shot baselines on proprietary and open-source agents, four training-free baselines including ground-truth-state prompting as an upper bound for annotator-based multi-agent approaches, StaR-style prompting vs. training, component ablations (Table 10), generalization checks on three agentic benchmarks, and a dynamic AndroidWorld-based evaluation with case studies.

The conclusion that structured state-aware reasoning must be learned via training rather than prompted is supported by the data, and the finding that StaR preserves or improves general agentic performance (with an honest error analysis of the AgentCPM-GUI outlier) adds credibility.
Reproducibility is reasonable: training hyperparameters, prompt templates for all agents and all baselines, metric definitions, and a stated commitment to release code and benchmark.
weaknesses: Label noise is non-trivial: the authors report only 91% state annotation accuracy (92.5% functionality) on a 200-sample manual check. For a benchmark whose core evaluation is a binary CLICK-vs-COMPLETE decision, roughly 9% noisy ground truth is material and complicates interpretation of the reported gains, particularly on negative samples.

The benchmark construction is partly circular and synthetically balanced: each screenshot is expanded into a positive and a negative instruction of near-templated form ('turn on/off {functionality}'). Real users rarely issue 'turn off' when the state already matches, so the heavy negative-sample distribution is artificial, and StaR-trained models may largely be learning this template rather than a general state-aware capability. Test instructions remain highly templated.

Severe distributional skew and potential contamination: 7,558 of 8,184 test samples come from AITW, and the benchmark sources (AITW, AITZ, AndroidControl, etc.) overlap with the pretraining/fine-tuning data of the evaluated open-source agents, weakening the zero-shot baseline claims.

The scope is narrow and the method is a fairly straightforward instantiation of existing ideas (structured chain-of-thought + fine-tuning; the paper itself cites CoAT [58] and similar reasoning-chain works). The delta over prior reasoning-chain training for GUI agents is incremental and mostly confined to toggles.
The dynamic real-world evaluation is only 20 tasks; differences such as OS-Atlas-7B 10/20 vs. 55/20 have very coarse granularity, and claims of 'real-world applicability' rest on thin evidence.

Presentation and consistency issues: the abstract's code/benchmark link is empty; repeated typos ('finshed()' in figures, 'Trun on alarm', 'OminiParser' vs. OmniParser, GUI-Odyssey cited as [34]/AndroidWorld in the appendix); some results only in bar charts without numeric values, hindering precise comparison.

Improvements are largest on the authors' own benchmark with templated instructions; gains on general agentic benchmarks are modest or mixed (e.g., AgentCPM-GUI-8B degradations on AITZ and GUI-Odyssey), so the practical significance beyond the toggle niche is not firmly established.

strengths: The paper identifies and systematically documents a concrete, previously underexplored failure mode of GUI agents: unreliable execution of toggle/state-control instructions (e.g., false-positive toggling when the current state already matches the desired state). The preliminary study over 9 agents (including GPT-5, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro) with eight fine-grained metrics is a useful empirical contribution to the community.

The state control benchmark is reasonably large (40,918 annotated toggles; 81,836 expanded samples) and is accompanied by a thoughtful quality analysis, including a theoretical treatment of inter-annotator agreement (Eqs. 5-6, Table 4) and manual verification of 200 samples (92.5% functionality / 91% state accuracy).

Experimental coverage is broad: four agent backbones (OS-Atlas, UI-TARS, AgentCPM-GUI, GUI-Owl), comparison against four training-free baselines (including a ground-truth-state oracle upper bound in Appendix B.1), component ablations (Table 10), three static agentic benchmarks, and a dynamic AndroidWorld-based evaluation with case studies. The finding that training is necessary (prompting and even GT-state prompting underperform StaR training) is convincingly demonstrated.

The method is shown to be model-agnostic and does not sacrifice general agentic performance (Figure 5, Figure 7, including error analysis of the AgentCPM degradation outlier in Appendix B.2). The dynamic-environment case study (Figures 8-9) provides an intuitive illustration of the failure and fix.
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed prompts (Appendix C), hyperparameters (Table 8), metric definitions, and a statement that code and benchmark will be released.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. StaR is essentially a hand-designed, templated chain-of-thought (perceive current state / infer desired state / compare-and-decide) learned via standard SFT. This is an incremental extension of existing chain-of-action-thought reasoning work (e.g., AITZ/CoAT [58], GUI-R1, AgentCPM-GUI); the conceptual insight is simple and the main value lies in the empirical study rather than a new technique.

Benchmark construction and potential data-provenance concerns. The benchmark is annotated by MLLMs (Qwen-2-VL-72B, GLM-4V) rather than humans, leaving ~9% state-label noise per the authors' own verification. More importantly, the source datasets (AITW, AMEX, AndroidControl, etc.) are already in the training data of several evaluated agents, so zero-shot numbers may be inflated, and the state-control test split is drawn from the same distribution as the StaR training split, making the headline 30% improvements partly in-distribution and raising memorization concerns.

Severe training-distribution imbalance: 68,380 of 73,652 training samples (~93%) come from AITW (Table 3), and instructions are templated ('turn on/off {feature}'). Consistent with this, negative-sample accuracy reaches near-ceiling (~96% N-AMR) after training, suggesting the benchmark may be too templated/easy to discriminate stronger state reasoning; generalization to natural, diverse instructions and unseen toggle styles is not directly evaluated.

Evaluation of proprietary agents may be handicapped: GPT-4o achieves P-AMR of only 6.60 and GPT-5 15.30 using the UI-TARS/OS-Atlas prompt formats, which likely disadvantages models without dedicated GUI grounding training; the 'below 50% including GPT-5' claim in the abstract should be interpreted with this protocol choice in mind.

Scope is narrow. Toggle control is one small facet of GUI interaction, and the paper restricts to binary toggles on mobile. The general-agentic gains are modest and partly reported only as bar charts (Figure 5) without exact numbers, and the dynamic benchmark contains only 20 tasks, limiting the strength of the real-world applicability claims.

Presentation issues that should be corrected: 'OminiParser' (should be OmniParser), 'finshed()' in Figure 6, 'Trun on alarm' in Table 7, GUI-Odyssey cited as [34] (AndroidWorld) in Appendix A.3, duplicate reference entries [34]/[35] for AndroidWorld, and occasional awkward phrasing. These are minor but numerous.
